Were our proud dreams to vanish like this? We had been placed “a little lower than the angels,” yet now we proved no better than insects that live a day. We had called ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and here we were, a “quintessence of dust.” We had mourned that the pyramids outlived the embalmed bodies of their builders. Yet the simple straw hut of a shepherd beside the road was built to last longer than the whole human race. How could we reconcile this miserable transformation with our earlier ambitions and our seemingly great abilities?

Suddenly a voice within me seemed to speak, clearly and distinctly: This was ordained from eternity. Since the empty universe first brought forth its burden, this hour and its fulfillment have been bound to the horses carrying Time onward. Would you reverse the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Almighty! Eternal, unchanging Necessity, forever weaving the unbreakable chain of events with your busy fingers! I will not protest against your actions. My human mind may be unable to accept that everything that exists is right; but because what exists must exist, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were born to submit and hope, rather than to enjoy.

Would the reader grow weary if I described every detail of our slow journey from Paris to Geneva? If I recorded our crowded miseries day by day in a journal, could my hand set them down, or language find words for all the forms of our suffering, one dreadful event jostling and pressing upon another? Be patient, reader! Whoever you are, wherever you live, whether you belong to a race of spirits or descend from some surviving couple and possess a human nature and an earthly home, you will read here of an extinct race's deeds. You will wonder whether those who endured these recorded sufferings were made of fragile flesh and delicate bodies like your own. They certainly were. Weep, then, for surely, solitary being, your nature will be gentle. Shed compassionate tears, but listen as well to the story, and learn what your predecessors did and suffered.

Yet the final events of our passage through France were so filled with uncanny horror and bleak misery that I dare not linger over them. If I examined each incident separately, every fraction of a second would hold a harrowing story, its slightest word enough to freeze the blood in your young veins. It is right that I should build this memorial to the vanished race for your instruction; it is not right that I should drag you through hospital wards or the hidden rooms where the dead are kept.

“Yes, burglary tools. You seem very relieved to hear that. But what startled you so much? What did you expect we'd found?”

Huck was trapped. The old man's questioning eyes were fixed on him, and he would have given anything for a believable answer. Nothing came to mind. The gaze grew more and more searching. At last a ridiculous reply occurred to him; with no time to consider it, he took a chance and said weakly:

“Sunday school books, maybe.”

Poor Huck was too upset even to smile, but the old man burst into loud, delighted laughter that shook him from head to foot. When he finished, he said a laugh like that put money in a man's pocket by saving him a fortune in doctors' bills. Then he added:

“Poor fellow, you're pale and worn out. You're not well at all. No wonder you're a bit confused and unsettled. But you'll recover. Rest and sleep should put you right again, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed with himself for acting so foolishly and showing such suspicious excitement. Ever since overhearing the conversation at the widow's stile, he had given up thinking that the parcel from the tavern contained the treasure. But he had only believed it wasn't the treasure; he had never known for certain. That was why hearing about a recovered bundle had shaken his self-control. On balance, though, he was glad the incident had happened. Now he knew beyond any doubt that their bundle was not the bundle, and his mind felt peaceful and wonderfully comfortable. In fact, everything now seemed to be moving exactly as it should. The treasure must still be in Number 2. The men would be caught and jailed that day, leaving him and Tom free to take the gold that night without trouble or fear of interruption.

Just as they finished breakfast, someone knocked at the door. Huck darted into hiding, wanting no connection, however slight, with what had happened. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and noticed groups of townspeople coming up the hill to stare at the stile. Clearly the news had spread. He had to tell his visitors the story of the night, and the widow openly expressed her gratitude for being saved.

“Don't mention it, ma'am. There's someone else you may owe more to than you do to me and my boys, but he won't let me give you his name. Without him, we wouldn't have been there.”

Each witness compares it to a speaker of a language he does not know, rather than one he understands. The Frenchman thinks it was a Spaniard's voice, and says he ‘might have recognized some words if he knew Spanish.’ The Dutchman insists it belonged to a Frenchman. Yet we are told that, ‘because this witness does not understand French, he was questioned through an interpreter.’ The Englishman believes it was a German voice, though he ‘does not understand German.’ The Spaniard ‘is certain’ it was an Englishman, but judges entirely ‘by the tone,’ since ‘he knows no English.’ The Italian thinks it was a Russian, although he ‘has never spoken with anyone from Russia.’ A second Frenchman disagrees with the first and is sure the speaker was Italian. But he does not know Italian, and, like the Spaniard, bases his certainty on the tone. How extraordinarily strange that voice must have been to produce evidence like this! People from five major divisions of Europe could recognize nothing familiar even in its tones. You may suggest that it belonged to someone from Asia or Africa. There are few Asians or Africans in Paris, but without dismissing that possibility, I ask you to notice three things. One witness describes the voice as ‘harsh rather than high-pitched.’ Two others call it ‘rapid and uneven.’ None of the witnesses could identify any words, or even any sounds that resembled words.

“I do not know,” Dupin continued, “what you have made of my argument so far. But I can confidently say that sound reasoning from this part of the evidence alone—the testimony about the deep and high-pitched voices—is enough to raise a suspicion that should guide every further step in investigating the mystery. Even ‘sound reasoning’ does not fully express what I mean. These are the only conclusions that can properly be drawn, and they lead inevitably to one particular suspicion. I will not yet tell you what that suspicion is. For now, just remember that it was strong enough to give my examination of the room a definite purpose and direction.

“Let us now imagine that we are inside that room. What should we look for first? The way the murderers got out. I think I can safely say that neither of us believes in supernatural events.”
